answer.exemplar: The arc length of a central angle is not fixed by the size of the angle alone, because the same angle opens a longer arc on a bigger circle. What the formula s equals r times theta says is that the length of arc per unit of radius is always equal to the angle itself, and that statement is only true when the angle is counted in radians. One radian is defined as the angle that cuts an arc whose length equals the radius, so one radian always produces an arc of length r, two radians produce an arc of length 2r, and a whole turn of 2 pi radians produces the full circumference of 2 pi r. If the angle is measured in degrees the proportionality constant disappears, because a degree is one three hundred and sixtieth of a turn and not a length. That is why s equals r times theta with theta in radians needs no extra factor, while the degree version needs the factor pi over 180. Working the other way round, the formula can be read as defining the radian: the angle in radians is exactly the arc length divided by the radius, which is a dimensionless ratio and so can be compared with an ordinary number.

questions.explanation: A good answer here connects the definition of the radian to the formula rather than asserting it. The radian is the angle that cuts an arc of length equal to the radius, which makes the arc length a plain product of the radius and the angle, with no constant attached. In degrees that product is wrong by the factor of pi over 180, so a student who multiplies 6 by 40 gets 240 units when the arc is really about 4.19, an error by a factor of about 57.
questions.hint: Begin with the definition of one radian and let the formula follow from it.

answer.exemplar: The law of sines works in one direction only. Given a side and its opposite angle it hands back a ratio, and from that ratio it hands back the sine of a second angle rather than the angle itself. Inside the range from 0 to 180 degrees every sine value in that range is taken twice, once on the way up and once on the way down, so a single sine always carries two candidate angles, an acute one and its supplement. The example in this question makes that concrete: the sine of B comes out as 0.8, so B is either 53.13 degrees or 126.87 degrees, and after setting aside the 30 degrees of angle A both candidates still leave a positive third angle, which is the test that keeps or rejects each one. Two triangles therefore share the same three measurements while differing in shape, and that is why the data given here do not determine a unique triangle. The law of cosines escapes the problem because it never passes through an inverse sine: the side appears only as a square, so the equation is a quadratic in that side with at most one positive root, and the shape is fixed by the included angle rather than left in two branches.

questions.explanation: A strong answer points at the inverse sine as the source of the problem. Each sine in the range from 0 to 1 belongs to two angles between 0 and 180 degrees, so the second candidate is the supplement of the first, and the two give genuinely different shapes with the same three measurements. The test is whether the candidate angle plus the known angle still leaves a positive third angle; the law of cosines has no such branch because it solves for a squared side and the included angle is stated directly.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of inverse operation the law performs, and where a second answer could come from.

answer.exemplar: The dot product of two vectors is defined as the magnitude of the first times the magnitude of the second times the cosine of the angle between them, so dividing the dot product by the product of the two magnitudes recovers that cosine and nothing else. A dot product of exactly zero therefore forces the cosine to be zero, provided both magnitudes are nonzero, and the only angle in the usual range whose cosine is zero is 90 degrees, so the two vectors are perpendicular. It does not follow that either vector is zero, and it does not say anything about their lengths, which can be any positive values at all. The same identity explains the whole sign scheme: a positive dot product means an acute angle, a negative one an obtuse angle, and a positive result is also what two parallel vectors in the same direction produce, since their cosine is 1 and the dot product is then just the product of the magnitudes. So a zero dot product separates perpendicular from every other case, while a large positive value on its own cannot separate parallel from merely close together, because a large magnitude will produce a large product in either case.

questions.explanation: A complete answer divides the dot product by the two magnitudes to reach the cosine, and then notes that a cosine of zero means a right angle. It should also be explicit about the limits: nothing follows about the lengths of the two vectors, and neither of them can be the zero vector, since a zero vector has no direction to compare. Worth adding that a large positive dot product cannot by itself distinguish parallel vectors from merely well-aligned ones.
questions.hint: Start from the definition that a dot product is a product of two magnitudes and a cosine.

answer.exemplar: The amplitude and the range answer different questions, and the difference between them is exactly the amount the graph has been lifted or lowered. The amplitude is the factor multiplying the cosine, so for 4 times the cosine of 2x the amplitude is 4, and it says the graph swings four units above and four units below whatever height it is centred on. It says nothing about where that centre sits. The range comes from the bounds of the cosine itself, which run from -1 to 1, so the whole function runs from 4 times -1 less 1 to 4 times 1 less 1, which is from -5 to 3. The two figures differ because the graph has been shifted down by 1, and a vertical shift moves the range bodily without changing the amplitude. The coefficient 2 on the angle does not appear in either figure: it compresses the graph horizontally and changes the period, which is 2 pi over 2, or pi, without touching the height at all. A common confusion is to report the amplitude as 5, which is the distance from the lowest point to the highest, and that number is really the length of the range.

questions.explanation: The explanation should separate the three ingredients of the form: the coefficient sets the amplitude at 4, the coefficient on the angle sets the period at pi, and the number outside shifts the midline down to -1. Since the cosine runs from -1 to 1, the function runs from -5 to 3, so the range is 8 wide while the amplitude is 4. Naming 5 as the amplitude, or letting the 2 on the angle affect the height, would both show the ingredients have been confused.
questions.hint: Deal with the coefficient, the shift, and the coefficient on the angle one at a time.
